title: FROM PRISONER TO PRIME MINISTER
paragraphs: The chains rattled every time he moved.
The damp walls of the Egyptian prison did not care whether Joseph was innocent. The darkness did not care about his dreams. The iron bars did not care about the promises God had spoken over his life.
And if we're honest, that is where many people secretly live today.
But in a prison of betrayal.
A prison of wondering why God allowed something they never deserved.
Joseph's story begins with a scandal.
A scandal that nearly destroyed his life.
Yet this is precisely where the Gospel begins to shine.
Because God specializes in taking the chapter that should have ended your story and turning it into the beginning of His.
Joseph was the favored son of Jacob. In Hebrew, his name is יוֹסֵף (Yosef), meaning "May He add" or "He will increase."
The name itself carried prophetic weight.
Before the palace came the pit.
His brothers hated him. Every dream he shared seemed to deepen their resentment. Eventually they stripped him of his robe, threw him into a pit, and sold him into slavery.
The realization that your own family is responsible.
The people who should have protected you became the people who wounded you.
Not every betrayal comes from strangers.
The deepest wounds often come from those closest to us.
Joseph's brothers staged his death and carried the deception home.
Years later Joseph found himself serving in the house of Potiphar. Despite everything, Genesis repeatedly declares:
Those words are easy to celebrate when life is working.
They become revolutionary when life is falling apart.
Because God's presence is not proven by comfort.
God's presence is often revealed through endurance.
Joseph prospered because God was with him.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him.
His response reveals one of Scripture's most remarkable statements:
"How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9)
Notice what he did not say.
He did not say, "I might get caught."
He did not say, "This could hurt my reputation."
He saw sin vertically before he saw it horizontally.
Eventually Potiphar's wife fabricated a story.
Joseph became the victim of a false accusation.
The innocent man was treated as guilty.
The righteous man became a prisoner.
The faithful servant became a criminal.
The Hebrew text describes Joseph being cast into the "בֵּית הַסֹּהַר" (Beit HaSohar), literally "the house of confinement."
Yet even there, Scripture repeats the same astonishing truth:
What if the greatest miracle in your suffering is not immediate deliverance?
What if the miracle is that God never left?
Many believers assume God's faithfulness means avoiding hardship.
God was faithful in the pit.
And God was preparing something Joseph could not yet see.
One moment particularly hurts to read.
Joseph interpreted the cupbearer's dream correctly and asked him to remember him before Pharaoh.
How many people know that feeling?
The person who promised help and vanished.
The prayer that seems suspended somewhere between earth and heaven.
Yet disappointment never altered God's plan.
Heaven's timing often feels painfully slow because God is shaping more than circumstances.
Pharaoh had troubling dreams nobody could interpret.
The prisoner was brought before the king.
And now a single conversation would change history.
When Pharaoh asked for an interpretation, Joseph's answer revealed his character:
"It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer."
After everything Joseph endured, he still refused to steal God's glory.
His confidence was rooted in God's power, not his own ability.
Seven years of abundance would be followed by seven years of famine.
He then proposed a strategy that would preserve Egypt.
"Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?"
Even a pagan ruler could see evidence of God's presence in Joseph.
Not because Joseph carried a title.
Then came one of the most dramatic reversals in Scripture.
The promotion was so astonishing that Pharaoh placed his own signet ring upon Joseph's hand and elevated him over the entire nation.
Only Pharaoh himself possessed greater authority.
What looked like the end had become the beginning.
But the most powerful moment of Joseph's story was still ahead.
The famine eventually brought Joseph's brothers to Egypt.
The very men who sold him now stood before him.
Joseph possessed the power to destroy them.
No court would have questioned it.
No witness would have defended them.
No one would have blamed him.
This was the perfect opportunity for revenge.
Instead, it became the stage for grace.
The emotional climax arrives in Genesis 45.
Not because he finally had power.
Then comes one of the most profound declarations in all of Scripture:
"You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." (Genesis 50:20)
The Hebrew word translated "meant" is חָשַׁב (chashav).
It carries the idea of weaving, planning, designing, or crafting.
This does not mean evil becomes good.
It means God is so sovereign that even evil cannot stop His purposes.
The cross proves this more clearly than anything else.
Like Joseph, Jesus was betrayed by those close to Him.
Like Joseph, Jesus was falsely accused.
Like Joseph, Jesus was rejected despite innocence.
Like Joseph, Jesus suffered although He was righteous.
But where Joseph's suffering preserved a nation from physical famine, Christ's suffering rescues sinners from eternal separation from God.
The Greek word used throughout the New Testament for grace is χάρις (charis).
That is exactly what Joseph extended to his brothers.
And it is exactly what Christ extends to us.
The greatest scandal in history is not that Joseph was falsely accused.
It is that sinful humanity rebelled against a holy God.
The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 5:8:
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we fixed our failures.
The Gospel is not the story of people reaching God.
The Gospel is the story of God reaching people.
Many readers are still living somewhere between the pit and the palace.
Between the promise and the fulfillment.
Between the betrayal and the breakthrough.
Between the prison and the promotion.
Joseph's story reminds us that God is working even when we cannot see it.
None of it is wasted in the hands of God.
The same God who guided Joseph through betrayal, slavery, false accusation, imprisonment, and promotion is still writing stories today.
Perhaps your life currently feels more like a prison than a palace.
Perhaps you carry wounds nobody sees.
Perhaps somebody else's decision changed the course of your life.
Perhaps you've been waiting longer than you expected.
The Aramaic language spoken in Jesus' earthly world preserved a word that captures His invitation beautifully: ܐܒܐ (Abba).
The God who walked with Joseph through prison is the same Father who walks with His children through every valley.
And if He could transform a prisoner into a prime minister, He can transform your story as well.
Because the Gospel has always been about transformation.
Take a moment and be honest.
Where are you in Joseph's story?
And if you know someone currently walking through betrayal, disappointment, or a season of waiting, share this with them.
They may need the reminder that God's silence is not His absence.
The prison was never the end of Joseph's story; it was the hallway God used to lead him to his purpose.
